questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# CONTROLROOM — dense monospace ops dashboard

**Source:** `~/Code/pds/dashboard/src/styles.css`
**Use for:** operational dashboards, queue/job boards, log viewers, internal tools. Anything where information density beats polish.

## Feel

All-monospace, 13px, cool near-black. Flat panels separated by hairlines, no shadows, no animation. Colored left-borders and border-color carry state. Reads like a terminal that grew a layout.

## Fonts

```css
font: 13px/1.5 ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, monospace;
```

One font, one size. Hierarchy comes from color and weight, not scale.

## Tokens

```css
:root {
  --bg:#0f1117; --panel:#171a23; --panel2:#12141c; --sel:#1f2430;
  --fg:#d7dce5; --dim:#7b8494; --line:#262b38;
  --purple:#a78bfa;  /* brand / primary action */
  --lit:#fb923c;     /* orange — in-progress, active, needs-you */
  --ok:#4ade80;      /* green — succeeded */
  --bad:#f87171;     /* red — failed, blocked, dead */
}
```

Semantic pairs for filled badges and diff lines (hand-picked, not tokens):

```
blocked/reject  bg #7f1d1d  fg #fecaca
running/changes bg #78350f  fg #fde68a
done/accept     bg #064e3b  fg #a7f3d0
waiting         bg #1e293b  fg var(--dim)
diff add        bg #062e1f  fg #a7f3d0
diff del        bg #2e0d0d  fg #fecaca
diff hunk       fg #7dd3fc
alert surface   bg #450a0a / #1a0f0f, border #7f1d1d
```

## Layout

```
.app       max-width 1400px, margin auto, padding 16px
header     flex space-between, 1px --line bottom rule
h2         13px UPPERCASE, .08em tracking, --dim   ← section labels, same size as body
h3         12px --dim
.kanban    grid, repeat(7,1fr), gap 8px
.col       --panel2 fill, 1px --line, radius 8px, padding 8px
.card      --panel fill, radius 6px, padding 8px; hover → border --lit
.metrics   flex row of .metric (radius 8, min-width 90) — b is 20px, span is 11px --dim
.row       flex, gap 12, 1px --line bottom; .done/.bad/.dead recolor the whole row
.logs      max-height 340, overflow auto; .log is 11px flex [ev | jid | data]
```

## State grammar

- **Border color** = state on a container: `.card.running` → `--lit`, `.card.blocked` → `--bad`, `.step.done` → `--ok`.
- **3px left border** = state on a list/group row: `.step-group.done|.dead|.leased`, `.finding.high|.medium`.
- **`.badge`** = 10px pill, uppercase, `.05em` — filled from the semantic pairs above.
- **Text color** = state on a whole row: `.row.done` green, `.row.bad` red.

## Component vocabulary

`.kanban/.col/.card` board · `.flow/.step` pipeline strip (clickable, `.selected` → `--sel`) · `.history/.step-group` collapsible `<details>` · `.logs/.log` stream · `.interrupts-banner/.intr` alert stack · `.resolve` prompt form · `.review/.finding` verdict panel · `.changes/.difffiles/.filediff/.diff/.dl` per-file collapsible diff · `.verdict/.verdict-btns` accept/changes/reject · `.capture` input bar · `.job-ctl` inline row controls (`.danger` → red) · `.play`/`.play-batch` purple advance buttons.

## Rules

- Radii 5–10px. Buttons and inputs at 6px, panels at 8–10px.
- Buttons: `--panel` fill + `--line` border by default; `.ghost` is transparent + `--lit` text; primary is filled `--lit` or `--purple` with near-black text.
- No shadows, no transitions, no hover lift. Only `border-color` changes on hover.
- Long error strings truncate to one line and expand on click (`.dlq-row .err.open`) — a stack trace must never inflate a row.
- Dark only. No light mode, no theme toggle.

# Bastion plan

Bastion is a harness and a factory for agent work, on the iii engine. A
request goes in, a reviewed change comes out, and nothing merges itself. What
Bastion adds is governance you can measure: constraints and capabilities built
into the harness's hooks, a way to promote and demote each one, a
tamper-evident audit record, and A/B evals that show what a change to the
harness does. It is one app: a Tauri 2 window with a Leptos frontend and a Rust
core, against a local engine that the app starts. A remote engine on the
owner's own box comes later (§10). Written 2026-10-30, revised the same day.

It is general. The owner sets up their own accounts and settings so Bastion
uses the processes, products, tools and policies they already use: their forge,
their tracker, their CI, their model providers, their pipeline and their rules.

**The words** (used the same way everywhere in Bastion):

- **Charter:** a project's own rules, written by people and kept in the
  project: its `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and the constraints and capabilities
  it declares. Each workspace has a charter, or runs without one on the owner's
  defaults.
- **Harness:** what runs one agent turn and applies the charter to it. Hooks
  check each call against the constraints and capabilities in force. Bastion is
  a harness.
- **Factory:** the pipeline of stages and checkpoints that turns a request into
  a landed change, with turns in the harness at its agent stages. Bastion is a
  factory.
- **Constraint:** a rule about what a turn must or must not do, on a ladder:
  told (in the brief), checked (a hook records breaches), enforced (a hook
  refuses the call).
- **Capability:** a function a turn may call, on a ladder: denied, ask (the
  call waits for the owner), allowed.
- **Promote, demote:** move one constraint or capability one rung, as a
  recorded decision the owner can back with an eval.

The **job** is the main idea: one request, like a ticket. The app reads like
GitHub Actions and like wipp's Jobs page. The first view lists every job, with
the ones waiting on the owner first. A job's page shows its pipeline as steps,
each with its state, its artifacts and its agent turns, and a panel at the top
when the job needs the owner. Antigravity starts at the agent; Bastion starts
at the job.

Bastion reaches feature parity with wipp (`~/Code/wipp`, as of commit
`f7c7e02`): every feature wipp has, except the ones tied to hosting and to
more than one user (§7.1). Parity is at the level of features, not code: wipp
runs Claude Code in sprites.dev VMs, and Bastion runs `harness` turns in
`iii-sandbox` VMs.

Bastion is not an editor. The owner keeps their own editor. The one view of
code inside Bastion is the diff a job proposes.

## 1. Goals

1. One native app on macOS and Linux runs Bastion against a local `iii` engine.
   No terminal is needed after install.
2. The Jobs page lists every job with its state and stage, the ones waiting
   on the owner first. The job page shows each step of its pipeline, as a run
   of GitHub Actions does. Both update by push.
3. A job moves through a **pipeline** of stages. Agents do the work in each
   stage, several jobs at once, each in its own worktree and sandbox VM.
4. Every stage leaves an **artifact** a person can judge: a plan, a test
   result, a diff, a screenshot, a recording or a briefing. A comment on an
   artifact goes back to the agent as its next instruction.
5. An agent can drive a browser, and its screenshots and recordings are
   artifacts.
6. Nothing merges itself. A person decides every merge.
7. A job that needs the owner raises a native notification within 2 s.
8. No Bastion process serves HTTP. The engine listens on loopback only.
9. Feature parity with wipp, with the exceptions §7.1 names.
10. Every constraint and capability is a hook decision, so an eval of two
    harness configurations shows a difference in behavior the owner can act on.
11. The audit record detects any change to a past entry.
12. Forge, tracker, CI, model providers, notifications, pipeline and policies
    are the owner's settings, not built in.

## 2. Non-goals

- Not an editor or a file browser. The diff artifact is the only view of code.
  "Open in editor" hands a worktree path to the owner's own editor.
- Not an agent chat. The owner talks to a job through its artifacts and
  checkpoints, not through a prompt box per agent.
- Not a browser app, and no HTTP API.
- Not multi-user. One owner, on their own machine. No sign-in. This drops
  wipp's accounts, GitHub sign-in, org check and roles (§7.1).
- Not a new agent runtime. Turns run on the stock `harness`, `llm-router` and
  `iii-sandbox` workers.
- Not hosted. wipp runs on Fly for a GitHub org, behind Caddy. Bastion runs
  on the owner's machine, so the Fly deploy is not ported (§7.1).
- Not a remote client yet. The owner's box is §10.
- Not Windows. Sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.

## 3. Fixed decisions

| # | Decision | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D1 | Rust for all Bastion code. TypeScript or JavaScript only where no Rust path exists, and each such file is named in §4 with its reason. | One language. |
| D2 | Tauri 2, the stable line. `cargo search` shows 3.0.0-alpha.5 on 2026-10-30, so 3 waits. | A native app with a Rust core. |
| D3 | The frontend is Leptos 0.8, client-side rendered to WASM and built by Trunk. | Rust pages in Tauri's webview. |
| D4 | One dark theme, purple as the main color (`--primary: #7c3aed`, `--primary-hover: #6d28d9`, `--link: #c4b5fd`). No light theme. Tailwind 4 runs as Trunk's standalone binary. | The owner's choice. No Node toolchain. |
| D5 | One Cargo workspace: the frontend crate at the root, the app in `src-tauri/`, shared code in `crates/`, Bastion workers in `workers/` (§4). | One build, one lockfile, one CI. |
| D6 | Every Bastion worker is a Rust binary on `iii-sdk` 0.25.0. Compose starts it through `scripts.run`. | The same engine, with no second runtime. |
| D7 | A stock registry worker comes first. Bastion writes a worker only for what no pinned worker does, and §5 records each choice. | Less code to own. The stack already pins `harness`, `iii-sandbox`, `worktree`, `approval-gate`, `workflow`, `session-manager`, `github` and `storage`. |
| D8 | Bastion's records (jobs, stages, artifacts, comments, decisions) live in the `database` worker as typed columns. Each row carries a `rev`, and a stale write is refused. | wipp lost a live job in the `state` worker on restart, and a last write once overrode a Stop. |
| D9 | The pages reach the engine only through typed Tauri commands. A command maps to one engine function or one core routine, and no command takes a function id. | One narrow surface, listed in one file. |
| D10 | Live updates are push. The engine adapter observes engine events (a turn completed, a CI run changed) by push. After each change it persists, the app emits a Tauri event `{kind, id, revision}`, and the page reads the resource again. | wipp polled. Push needs no timers and no stale views. |
| D11 | One owner, no sign-in. The actor on every record is `git config user.name`. The owner's accounts with other services (forge, tracker, providers) are settings, kept in `secrets` (A7). | One person on one machine needs no accounts. |
| D12 | Local is the default and only mode for now. The engine address is a profile field, never a constant. | The remote box (§10) becomes a new profile kind, not a rewrite. |
| D13 | The app starts the stack with `iii compose --up -f worker-compose.yaml`, and attaches to a stack that already runs. On quit, the owner chooses whether it keeps running. | The owner's choice. No terminal. |
| D14 | Every agent turn runs in an `iii-sandbox` VM on its job's worktree. A credential never enters the VM. Pushes and PRs happen on the host. | wipp's lesson: a sprite that saw a credential is tainted. |
| D15 | Merge is a person's decision, or `hold` at the lowest. Every other checkpoint has a dial: `ask`, `hold` (default after 30 min) or `auto`. | wipp's oversight model. |
| D16 | A comment on an artifact goes to the agent verbatim, as its next brief. A fix loop stops after a set count, or sooner when a refusal repeats word for word. | wipp's bounded loops. Paraphrased feedback loses the point. |
| D17 | Every job runs a pipeline. The smallest pipeline is plan, approve, build, review, land, and it is the default until A8 adds the rest. | The factory is the unit. A free-form task is a short pipeline, not a second mode. |
| D18 | All factory logic lives in the app, in `crates/bastion-core`, apart from the view and from iii (§6.1). The core takes an event and the current state, and returns the new state and a list of effects. It does no I/O, has no `async`, and does not depend on `iii-sdk`, Tauri or Leptos. | The owner's choice. The rules are tested as plain functions, with no engine and no window. |
| D19 | The seams in §6.2 are the only ways across layers, and Cargo dependencies enforce them. A CI check fails if `bastion-protocol` gains a dependency other than `serde`, if `bastion-core` gains one other than `serde` and `sha2` (for the audit chain, D21), or if `iii-sdk` is imported outside `src-tauri/src/engine/`. | The owner wants clean seams. A seam that only a reviewer guards erodes. |
| D20 | Every constraint and capability is enforced in a harness hook, and its ladder position is data. A turn's behavior changes only through those hooks and that data. | An eval can then name what changed. A rule kept only in a prompt cannot be measured. |
| D21 | The audit record is a hash chain with one writer. Each entry carries an HMAC-SHA256 of its fields and the entry before it, keyed with a secret kept in the macOS Keychain, not in the record, and verification walks the chain. | Any change to a past entry breaks the chain, and whoever can edit the database cannot recompute it without the Keychain key. It still cannot stop a change, or detect entries cut from the end; a remote append-only copy (§10) closes that, later. |
| D22 | An eval compares two harness configurations on the same requests and the same workspace snapshots, and reports the difference with the hook decisions behind it. | A promotion or demotion comes with evidence, not a guess. |
| D23 | Forge, tracker, CI, model providers and notifications are adapters behind seams, chosen in Settings. A new product is a new adapter, not a core change. | The owner keeps the tools they already use. |
| D25 | Every constraint and capability belongs to one layer. The charter is the repository's own, read from it (`.claude/settings.json` today). The harness runs an agent's turn and binds its calls. The factory moves a job through its pipeline and binds review, land, pull requests and merges. The Constraints and Capabilities pages each show the three. | The owner's words: a charter belongs to a repo, and the harness and factory are Bastion's, built on iii. A rule is easier to judge when its place is plain. |
| D26 | The owner changes the harness and the factory as data, with no code change. Their rules, grants and settings live in Bastion's database, served by the stack's `database` worker: the owner edits them on the pages, or directly in `data/bastion.db`, and the gate reads them again before each turn. The first-run defaults are a SQL file the stack carries (`seed/governance.sql`), not constants in Bastion's code. | The owner's choice (2026-10-31): the owner updates their own settings and configuration while the factory runs. Spike N11 showed the `configuration` worker could carry them as YAML; the owner chose the database, which keeps the rules, their history and the audit in one place. |
| D27 | Bastion is a server and its clients. `bastion-server`, one Rust binary on `axum` and `tokio`, is the source of truth: it holds the factory (`bastion-core` and its adapter), the store, the gate, the audit chain, the forge, and the stack on its machine. Business logic lives in the server; iii workers are the implementation under it, reached only through the Engine seam. A client shows state, sends the owner's actions and follows updates, and keeps no business state. Jobs advance with no app open, and one server serves the app on this machine or another. D18 kept the core pure, so it moves without change. |
| D28 | The API is HTTP with JSON. Each route is one action on one resource, its types live in `bastion-protocol`, and every request carries the Bastion server's bearer token. The view calls the server from the webview. Replaces D9's Tauri commands, except the few that belong to the window (S3). | One surface for every client, typed once. |
| D29 | Push is server-sent events. `GET /events` streams D10's `{kind, id, revision}` with an event id. A client that reconnects with `Last-Event-ID` gets what it missed, or a `resync` when it is too far behind, and then reads again. | D30 | The app keeps a list of Bastion servers the owner added, each a name, a base URL and a token kept in the Keychain. The server the app starts on this machine is `local`. A page about one server (Engine, Settings, Constraints, Capabilities, Audit Log, Evals) has a server picker at its top, `local` by default; the sidebar names no server. "Bastion server" is the one word for it: not target, not profile. Replaces D12's profiles. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06): use several backends at once, chosen job by job. |

## 6. Concepts

From the top down:

  and finished. Filter by workspace and search by text.
- **Job page:** one job as a run. The request, its state, the pipeline as
  steps with their artifacts and turns, and the owner's actions when it waits.
- **Workspace:** a repository the owner registers with Bastion.
- **Job:** one request against one workspace. It owns one worktree, one

- **Pipeline:** the stages a job moves through. It is data, so a job can run a

- **Stage:** one step of a pipeline. An agent stage runs one or more turns; a

- **Checkpoint:** a point where a person decides, with a dial (D15).

content.content:
1	# Bastion plan
2	
3	Bastion is a harness and a factory for agent work, on the iii engine. A
4	request goes in, a reviewed change comes out, and nothing merges itself. What
5	Bastion adds is governance you can measure: constraints and capabilities built
6	into the harness's hooks, a way to promote and demote each one, a
7	tamper-evident audit record, and A/B evals that show what a change to the
8	harness does. It is one app: a Tauri 2 window with a Leptos frontend and a Rust
9	core, against a local engine that the app starts. A remote engine on the
10	owner's own box comes later (§10). Written 2026-10-30, revised the same day.
11	
12	It is general. The owner sets up their own accounts and settings so Bastion
13	uses the processes, products, tools and policies they already use: their forge,
14	their tracker, their CI, their model providers, their pipeline and their rules.
15	
16	**The words** (used the same way everywhere in Bastion):
17	
18	- **Charter:** a project's own rules, written by people and kept in the
19	  project: its `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and the constraints and capabilities
20	  it declares. Each workspace has a charter, or runs without one on the owner's
21	  defaults.
22	- **Harness:** what runs one agent turn and applies the charter to it. Hooks
23	  check each call against the constraints and capabilities in force. Bastion is
24	  a harness.
25	- **Factory:** the pipeline of stages and checkpoints that turns a request into
26	  a landed change, with turns in the harness at its agent stages. Bastion is a
27	  factory.
28	- **Constraint:** a rule about what a turn must or must not do, on a ladder:
29	  told (in the brief), checked (a hook records breaches), enforced (a hook
30	  refuses the call).
31	- **Capability:** a function a turn may call, on a ladder: denied, ask (the
32	  call waits for the owner), allowed.
33	- **Promote, demote:** move one constraint or capability one rung, as a
34	  recorded decision the owner can back with an eval.
35	
36	The **job** is the main idea: one request, like a ticket. The app reads like
37	GitHub Actions and like wipp's Jobs page. The first view lists every job, with
38	the ones waiting on the owner first. A job's page shows its pipeline as steps,
39	each with its state, its artifacts and its agent turns, and a panel at the top
40	when the job needs the owner. Antigravity starts at the agent; Bastion starts
41	at the job.
42	
43	Bastion reaches feature parity with wipp (`~/Code/wipp`, as of commit
44	`f7c7e02`): every feature wipp has, except the ones tied to hosting and to
45	more than one user (§7.1). Parity is at the level of features, not code: wipp
46	runs Claude Code in sprites.dev VMs, and Bastion runs `harness` turns in
47	`iii-sandbox` VMs.
48	
49	Bastion is not an editor. The owner keeps their own editor. The one view of
50	code inside Bastion is the diff a job proposes.
51	
52	## 1. Goals
53	
54	1. One native app on macOS and Linux runs Bastion against a local `iii` engine.
55	   No terminal is needed after install.
56	2. The Jobs page lists every job with its state and stage, the ones waiting
57	   on the owner first. The job page shows each step of its pipeline, as a run
58	   of GitHub Actions does. Both update by push.
59	3. A job moves through a **pipeline** of stages. Agents do the work in each
60	   stage, several jobs at once, each in its own worktree and sandbox VM.
61	4. Every stage leaves an **artifact** a person can judge: a plan, a test
62	   result, a diff, a screenshot, a recording or a briefing. A comment on an
63	   artifact goes back to the agent as its next instruction.
64	5. An agent can drive a browser, and its screenshots and recordings are
65	   artifacts.
66	6. Nothing merges itself. A person decides every merge.
67	7. A job that needs the owner raises a native notification within 2 s.
68	8. No Bastion process serves HTTP. The engine listens on loopback only.
69	9. Feature parity with wipp, with the exceptions §7.1 names.
70	10. Every constraint and capability is a hook decision, so an eval of two
71	    harness configurations shows a difference in behavior the owner can act on.
72	11. The audit record detects any change to a past entry.
73	12. Forge, tracker, CI, model providers, notifications, pipeline and policies
74	    are the owner's settings, not built in.
75	
76	## 2. Non-goals
77	
78	- Not an editor or a file browser. The diff artifact is the only view of code.
79	  "Open in editor" hands a worktree path to the owner's own editor.
80	- Not an agent chat. The owner talks to a job through its artifacts and
81	  checkpoints, not through a prompt box per agent.
82	- Not a browser app, and no HTTP API.
83	- Not multi-user. One owner, on their own machine. No sign-in. This drops
84	  wipp's accounts, GitHub sign-in, org check and roles (§7.1).
85	- Not a new agent runtime. Turns run on the stock `harness`, `llm-router` and
86	  `iii-sandbox` workers.
87	- Not hosted. wipp runs on Fly for a GitHub org, behind Caddy. Bastion runs
88	  on the owner's machine, so the Fly deploy is not ported (§7.1).
89	- Not a remote client yet. The owner's box is §10.
90	- Not Windows. Sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with `/dev/kvm`.
91	
92	## 3. Fixed decisions
93	
94	| # | Decision | Why |
95	|---|---|---|
96	| D1 | Rust for all Bastion code. TypeScript or JavaScript only where no Rust path exists, and each such file is named in §4 with its reason. | One language. |
97	| D2 | Tauri 2, the stable line. `cargo search` shows 3.0.0-alpha.5 on 2026-10-30, so 3 waits. | A native app with a Rust core. |
98	| D3 | The frontend is Leptos 0.8, client-side rendered to WASM and built by Trunk. | Rust pages in Tauri's webview. |
99	| D4 | One dark theme, purple as the main color (`--primary: #7c3aed`, `--primary-hover: #6d28d9`, `--link: #c4b5fd`). No light theme. Tailwind 4 runs as Trunk's standalone binary. | The owner's choice. No Node toolchain. |
100	| D5 | One Cargo workspace: the frontend crate at the root, the app in `src-tauri/`, shared code in `crates/`, Bastion workers in `workers/` (§4). | One build, one lockfile, one CI. |
101	| D6 | Every Bastion worker is a Rust binary on `iii-sdk` 0.25.0. Compose starts it through `scripts.run`. | The same engine, with no second runtime. |
102	| D7 | A stock registry worker comes first. Bastion writes a worker only for what no pinned worker does, and §5 records each choice. | Less code to own. The stack already pins `harness`, `iii-sandbox`, `worktree`, `approval-gate`, `workflow`, `session-manager`, `github` and `storage`. |
103	| D8 | Bastion's records (jobs, stages, artifacts, comments, decisions) live in the `database` worker as typed columns. Each row carries a `rev`, and a stale write is refused. | wipp lost a live job in the `state` worker on restart, and a last write once overrode a Stop. |
104	| D9 | The pages reach the engine only through typed Tauri commands. A command maps to one engine function or one core routine, and no command takes a function id. | One narrow surface, listed in one file. |
105	| D10 | Live updates are push. The engine adapter observes engine events (a turn completed, a CI run changed) by push. After each change it persists, the app emits a Tauri event `{kind, id, revision}`, and the page reads the resource again. | wipp polled. Push needs no timers and no stale views. |
106	| D11 | One owner, no sign-in. The actor on every record is `git config user.name`. The owner's accounts with other services (forge, tracker, providers) are settings, kept in `secrets` (A7). | One person on one machine needs no accounts. |
107	| D12 | Local is the default and only mode for now. The engine address is a profile field, never a constant. | The remote box (§10) becomes a new profile kind, not a rewrite. |
108	| D13 | The app starts the stack with `iii compose --up -f worker-compose.yaml`, and attaches to a stack that already runs. On quit, the owner chooses whether it keeps running. | The owner's choice. No terminal. |
109	| D14 | Every agent turn runs in an `iii-sandbox` VM on its job's worktree. A credential never enters the VM. Pushes and PRs happen on the host. | wipp's lesson: a sprite that saw a credential is tainted. |
110	| D15 | Merge is a person's decision, or `hold` at the lowest. Every other checkpoint has a dial: `ask`, `hold` (default after 30 min) or `auto`. | wipp's oversight model. |
111	| D16 | A comment on an artifact goes to the agent verbatim, as its next brief. A fix loop stops after a set count, or sooner when a refusal repeats word for word. | wipp's bounded loops. Paraphrased feedback loses the point. |
112	| D17 | Every job runs a pipeline. The smallest pipeline is plan, approve, build, review, land, and it is the default until A8 adds the rest. | The factory is the unit. A free-form task is a short pipeline, not a second mode. |
113	| D18 | All factory logic lives in the app, in `crates/bastion-core`, apart from the view and from iii (§6.1). The core takes an event and the current state, and returns the new state and a list of effects. It does no I/O, has no `async`, and does not depend on `iii-sdk`, Tauri or Leptos. | The owner's choice. The rules are tested as plain functions, with no engine and no window. |
114	| D19 | The seams in §6.2 are the only ways across layers, and Cargo dependencies enforce them. A CI check fails if `bastion-protocol` gains a dependency other than `serde`, if `bastion-core` gains one other than `serde` and `sha2` (for the audit chain, D21), or if `iii-sdk` is imported outside `src-tauri/src/engine/`. | The owner wants clean seams. A seam that only a reviewer guards erodes. |
115	| D20 | Every constraint and capability is enforced in a harness hook, and its ladder position is data. A turn's behavior changes only through those hooks and that data. | An eval can then name what changed. A rule kept only in a prompt cannot be measured. |
116	| D21 | The audit record is a hash chain with one writer. Each entry carries an HMAC-SHA256 of its fields and the entry before it, keyed with a secret kept in the macOS Keychain, not in the record, and verification walks the chain. | Any change to a past entry breaks the chain, and whoever can edit the database cannot recompute it without the Keychain key. It still cannot stop a change, or detect entries cut from the end; a remote append-only copy (§10) closes that, later. |
117	| D22 | An eval compares two harness configurations on the same requests and the same workspace snapshots, and reports the difference with the hook decisions behind it. | A promotion or demotion comes with evidence, not a guess. |
118	| D23 | Forge, tracker, CI, model providers and notifications are adapters behind seams, chosen in Settings. A new product is a new adapter, not a core change. | The owner keeps the tools they already use. |
119	| D25 | Every constraint and capability belongs to one layer. The charter is the repository's own, read from it (`.claude/settings.json` today). The harness runs an agent's turn and binds its calls. The factory moves a job through its pipeline and binds review, land, pull requests and merges. The Constraints and Capabilities pages each show the three. | The owner's words: a charter belongs to a repo, and the harness and factory are Bastion's, built on iii. A rule is easier to judge when its place is plain. |
120	| D26 | The owner changes the harness and the factory as data, with no code change. Their rules, grants and settings live in Bastion's database, served by the stack's `database` worker: the owner edits them on the pages, or directly in `data/bastion.db`, and the gate reads them again before each turn. The first-run defaults are a SQL file the stack carries (`seed/governance.sql`), not constants in Bastion's code. | The owner's choice (2026-10-31): the owner updates their own settings and configuration while the factory runs. Spike N11 showed the `configuration` worker could carry them as YAML; the owner chose the database, which keeps the rules, their history and the audit in one place. |
121	| D27 | Bastion is a server and its clients. `bastion-server`, one Rust binary on `axum` and `tokio`, is the source of truth: it holds the factory (`bastion-core` and its adapter), the store, the gate, the audit chain, the forge, and the stack on its machine. Business logic lives in the server; iii workers are the implementation under it, reached only through the Engine seam. A client shows state, sends the owner's actions and follows updates, and keeps no business state. Replaces D18's "in the app", D13's app-owned stack, and §10's second adapter. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06). Jobs advance with no app open, and one server serves the app on this machine or another. D18 kept the core pure, so it moves without change. |
122	| D28 | The API is HTTP with JSON. Each route is one action on one resource, its types live in `bastion-protocol`, and every request carries the Bastion server's bearer token. The view calls the server from the webview. Replaces D9's Tauri commands, except the few that belong to the window (S3). | One surface for every client, typed once. |
123	| D29 | Push is server-sent events. `GET /events` streams D10's `{kind, id, revision}` with an event id. A client that reconnects with `Last-Event-ID` gets what it missed, or a `resync` when it is too far behind, and then reads again. The view reads the stream with `fetch`, so the token goes in a header. WebSockets wait until a client must stream to the server, such as a live terminal. | Push is one-way today. SSE is plain HTTP, so it passes the same token, proxy and SSH tunnel as the API. |
124	| D30 | The app keeps a list of Bastion servers the owner added, each a name, a base URL and a token kept in the Keychain. The server the app starts on this machine is `local`. A Bastion server holds its own workspaces, one per repository, each with its own setup, checks and tests. Each job runs on one Bastion server: New request picks the server, `local` by default, then one of its workspaces, and the job page names the server. Every server stays connected, and the Jobs page lists the jobs of all of them. A page about one server (Engine, Settings, Constraints, Capabilities, Audit Log, Evals) has a server picker at its top, `local` by default; the sidebar names no server. "Bastion server" is the one word for it: not target, not profile. Replaces D12's profiles. | The owner's choice (2026-11-06): use several backends at once, chosen job by job. |
125	
126	## 6. Concepts
127	
128	From the top down:
129	
130	- **Jobs page:** every job, in three groups: waiting for you, in progress,
131	  and finished. Filter by workspace and search by text.
132	- **Job page:** one job as a run. The request, its state, the pipeline as
133	  steps with their artifacts and turns, and the owner's actions when it waits.
134	- **Workspace:** a repository the owner registers with Bastion.
135	- **Job:** one request against one workspace. It owns one worktree, one
136	  sandbox VM and one pipeline run. States: `queued`, `running`, `needs_you`,
137	  `blocked`, `landed`, `closed`, `failed`, `stopped`.
138	- **Pipeline:** the stages a job moves through. It is data, so a job can run a
139	  short one or the full one.
140	- **Stage:** one step of a pipeline. An agent stage runs one or more turns; a
141	  person stage is a checkpoint.
142	- **Checkpoint:** a point where a person decides, with a dial (D15).
143	- **Artifact:** a typed output of a stage: plan, test result, diff,
144	  screenshot, recording, briefing. Bytes go to `storage`; the row goes to
145	  `database`.
146	- **Comment:** the owner's note on an artifact, or on one line of a diff. It
147	  becomes the stage's next brief (D16).
148	- **Turn:** one agent run inside a stage, with its transcript. The lowest
149	  level the app shows.
150	
151	### 6.1 Three layers
152	
153	| Layer | Where | Knows | Does not know |
154	|---|---|---|---|
155	| **Core** | `crates/bastion-core` | The factory's rules: which stage comes next, when a checkpoint waits, what the dial does, when a fix loop stops, what a brief says. | iii, Tauri, Leptos, the clock, the disk. |
156	| **Engine adapter** | `src-tauri/src/engine/` | How to run each effect on iii, and how to turn each engine event into a core event. It persists every new state with its `rev` (D8). | Any factory rule. |
157	| **View** | `src/` | How to draw a resource, and which typed command to call (D9). | iii and the factory's rules. |
158	
159	One loop joins them. An event arrives: the owner's decision through a command,
160	or an engine event such as a turn that completed. The adapter loads the job,
161	calls the core, writes the new state, runs the effects the core returned, and
162	emits the change to the page (D10). An effect is data, such as "start a turn
163	with this brief" or "open a PR". The core never waits on one.
164	
165	On start, the adapter reads every active job and resumes it. Read commands ask
166	the core for derived facts, such as which actions a checkpoint allows, so the
167	view never computes a rule itself.

# Bastion plan

Bastion is a harness and a factory for agent work, on the iii engine. A
request goes in, a reviewed change comes out, and nothing merges itself. What
Bastion adds is governance you can measure: constraints and capabilities built
into the harness's hooks, a way to promote and demote each one, a
tamper-evident audit record, and A/B evals that show what a change to the
harness does. It is one app: a Tauri 2 window with a Leptos frontend and a Rust
core, against a local engine that the app starts. A remote engine on the
owner's own box comes later (§10). Written 2026-10-30, revised the same day.

It is general. The owner sets up their own accounts and settings so Bastion
uses the processes, products, tools and policies they already use: their forge,
their tracker, their CI, their model providers, their pipeline and their rules.

**The words** (used the same way everywhere in Bastion):

- **Charter:** a project's own rules, written by people and kept in the
  project: its `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, and the constraints and capabilities
  it declares. Each workspace has a charter, or runs without one on the owner's
  defaults.
- **Harness:** what runs one agent turn and applies the charter to it. Hooks
  check each call against the constraints and capabilities in force. Bastion is
  a harness.
- **Factory:** the pipeline of stages and checkpoints that turns a request into
  a landed change, with turns in the harness at its agent stages. Bastion is a
  factory.
- **Constraint:** a rule about what a turn must or must not do, on a ladder:
  told (in the brief), checked (a hook records breaches), enforced (a hook
  refuses the call).
- **Capability:** a function a turn may call, on a ladder: denied, ask (the
  call waits for the owner), allowed.
- **Promote, demote:** move one constraint or capability one rung, as a
  recorded decision the owner can back with an eval.

The **job** is the main idea: one request, like a ticket. The app reads like
GitHub Actions and like wipp's Jobs page. The first view lists every job, with
the ones waiting on the owner first. A job's page shows its pipeline as steps,
each with its state, its artifacts and its agent turns, and a panel at the top
when the job needs the owner. Antigravity starts at the agent; Bastion starts
at the job.

Bastion reaches feature parity with wipp (`~/Code/wipp`, as of commit
`f7c7e02`): every feature wipp has, except the ones tied to hosting and to
more than one user (§7.1). Parity is at the level of features, not code: wipp
runs Claude Code in sprites.dev VMs, and Bastion runs `harness` turns in
`iii-sandbox` VMs.

Bastion is not an editor. The owner keeps their own editor. The one view of
code inside Bastion is the diff a job proposes.

## 1. Goals

1. One native app on macOS and Linux runs Bastion against a local `iii` engine.
   No terminal is needed after install.
2. The Jobs page lists every job with its state and stage, the ones waiting
   on the owner first. The job page shows each step of its pipeline, as a run
   of GitHub Actions does. Both update by push.
3. A job moves through a **pipeline** of stages. Agents do the work in each
   stage, several jobs at once, each in its own worktree and sandbox VM.
4. Every stage leaves an **artifact** a person can judge: a plan, a test
   result, a diff, a screenshot, a recording or a briefing. A comment on an
   artifact goes back to the agent as its next instruction.
5. An agent can drive a browser, and its screenshots and recordings are
   artifacts.
6. Nothing merges itself. A person decides every merge.
7. A job that needs the owner raises a native notification within 2 s.
8. No Bastion process serves HTTP. The engine listens on loopback only.
9. Feature parity with wipp, with the exceptions §7.1 names.
10. Every constraint and capability is a hook decision, so an eval of two
    harness configurations shows a difference in behavior the owner can act on.
11. The audit record detects any change to a past entry.
12. Forge, tracker, CI, model providers, notifications, pipeline and policies
    are the owner's settings, not built in.

## 2. Non-goals

- Not an editor or a file browser. The diff artifact is the only view of code.
  "Open in editor" hands a worktree path to the owner's own editor.
- Not an agent chat. The owner talks to a job through its artifacts and
  checkpoints, not through a prompt box per agent.
- Not a browser app, and no HTTP API.

## 6. Concepts

From the top down:

- **Jobs page:** every job, in three groups: waiting for you, in progress,
  and finished. Filter by workspace and search by text.
- **Job page:** one job as a run. The request, its state, the pipeline as
  steps with their artifacts and turns, and the owner's actions when it waits.
- **Workspace:** a repository the owner registers with Bastion.
- **Job:** one request against one workspace. It owns one worktree, one
  sandbox VM and one pipeline run. States: `queued`, `running`, `needs_you`,
  `blocked`, `landed`, `closed`, `failed`, `stopped`.
- **Pipeline:** the stages a job moves through. It is data, so a job can run a
  short one or the full one.
- **Stage:** one step of a pipeline. An agent stage runs one or more turns; a
  person stage is a checkpoint.
- **Checkpoint:** a point where a person decides, with a dial (D15).
- **Artifact:** a typed output of a stage: plan, test result, diff,
  screenshot, recording, briefing. Bytes go to `storage`; the row goes to
  `database`.
- **Comment:** the owner's note on an artifact, or on one line of a diff. It
  becomes the stage's next brief (D16).
- **Turn:** one agent run inside a stage, with its transcript. The lowest
  level the app shows.

### 6.1 Three layers

| Layer | Where | Knows | Does not know |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Core** | `crates/bastion-core` | The factory's rules: which stage comes next, when a checkpoint waits, what the dial does, when a fix loop stops, what a brief says. | iii, Tauri, Leptos, the clock, the disk. |
| **Engine adapter** | `src-tauri/src/engine/` | How to run each effect on iii, and how to turn each engine event into a core event. It persists every new state with its `rev` (D8). | Any factory rule. |
| **View** | `src/` | How to draw a resource, and which typed command to call (D9). | iii and the factory's rules. |

One loop joins them. An event arrives: the owner's decision through a command,
or an engine event such as a turn that completed. The adapter loads the job,
calls the core, writes the new state, runs the effects the core returned, and
emits the change to the page (D10). An effect is data, such as "start a turn
with this brief" or "open a PR". The core never waits on one.

On start, the adapter reads every active job and resumes it. Read commands ask
the core for derived facts, such as which actions a checkpoint allows, so the
view never computes a rule itself.

Found, and open: the Jobs page does not say when a server cannot be reached, and keeps showing its last read; stopping the background task that ran Two's server took its stack down too, and the job waiting at Approve lost its VM (`sandbox not found` at stop), so a job that waits across a stack restart cannot go on; whether a plan turn survives a kill mid-turn is not shown, because the plan finished too fast to tell; the add-server form keeps its values after Add. Then the Jobs page's unreachable server: the page now marks a server whose event stream is down, names it above the list, keeps that server's jobs as last read and marks them unreachable, and still says why a reachable server's jobs did not read; checked live by killing only Two's server, which put up the note, and restarting it, which cleared the note and brought Two's job back with no reload. Next: A8 step 4. |
| A9 to A13 | — | — |
| Later (§10) | on hold | — |

**What A1 found:**

- `iii-sdk` 0.25.0 reconnects by itself at a fixed delay, so the app adds no
  backoff. It reads `get_connection_state()` every 500 ms and pushes changes,
  because the SDK has no listener for it.
- `router::provider::list` says which providers have a credential, without the
  secret. So the provider check runs once the engine is up, and the machine
  checks run before it.
- `iii compose --up` is the compose daemon itself, in the foreground. The app
  starts it detached in its own process group, with its output in
  `compose.log` in the app's log directory. Run from a terminal, it stops when
  that terminal job stops, and so does the stack.
- The stack inherits the app's environment. A provider key set only in an
  interactive shell does not reach an app started some other way.
- `iii trigger` prints its answer and then does not exit.

**What A2 found:**

- `observe` watches only functions. `engine::functions-available` is a
  trigger type, so the app binds it with the deprecated `register_trigger`, as
  N3 does. It fires when a worker's functions join or leave, which is how a
  container's state reaches the page.
- compose reports `owned: false` for a container whose process is gone, so
  Start shows for any container that is not ready.
- Trunk watched the whole checkout, and the stack writes logs into it, so each
  log line rebuilt and reloaded the page. `Trunk.toml` now watches only what
  the view is built from.
- `bastion-steps` is still declared in `worker-compose.yaml`, though D18 left
  the factory with no queue.

**What A3 found so far:**

- `sandbox::create` cannot mount a host folder, so a job's branch goes into its
  VM as a git bundle and its commits come back the same way (N7).
- `harness::status` gives a finished turn's `result` and `result_error`, which
  is all the core needs, and it lets resume catch a turn that ended while the
  app was closed.
- `worktree::create` answers with `worktree_id`, and `worktree::land` reports
  only on its `worktree::landed` and `worktree::land-blocked` triggers.
- Each turn runs on gpt-5-mini through OpenAI until A9, because the stack has
  no Anthropic credential yet.
- `harness::status` truncates `result` and encodes it as a JSON string, so a
  turn's report comes from its last assistant message in `session::messages`.
- The bundle folder in the app's cache must exist before `git bundle create`.
- The factory starts after the page loads, so it announces itself with an
  empty `job-changed`, and every page reads again.
- Page reads overlap when pushes come fast, so each page keeps only its latest
  read. An artifact is written before the page hears of a change, so a panel
  that mounts on that change sees it.

**What A4 found:**

- An agent's report can claim work its commits do not hold. The diff from the
  VM is the ground truth, and work left uncommitted is listed at review.
- gpt-5-mini sometimes ended a turn by announcing its next step, ran tests
  through `bash -lc` (which hung the VM call), and passed no timeout, so one
  turn stalled for about 25 minutes. `harness` has no way to stop a turn. The
  turn guide now covers all three, and A5's constraints should enforce them:
  commit every change, keep existing tests, leave a clean tree.
- `git bundle create … HEAD` names no branch, so the pull found nothing. The
  bundle names the branch now.
- `worktree::land` needs `target_branch`, refuses a dirty target, and reports
  through `worktree::land-blocked` with a `reason`.

content.content:
Σ sigma 
 · coding agent 
 
 A reliable coding-agent CLI in Go: Claude Code in capability,
 hexagonal in philosophy, extras shipped as plugins — with a built-in A/B
 eval harness for testing changes with real data. 
 Sigma's premise: an agent becomes reliable when its output is
 constrained by layers you compose — sensors (observe),
 guides (steer), and gates (permit / deny / validate). Every
 layer is a small typed adapter behind a narrow port. It authenticates with
 an OpenAI API key from the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable. 
 Install 
 git clone https://github.com/tacoda/sigma
cd sigma
make build # -> bin/sigma 
 Requires Go 1.25+ and an OpenAI API key exported as OPENAI_API_KEY . 
 Quickstart 
 sigma auth status # verify OPENAI_API_KEY is set
sigma init # scaffold a starter .sigma/ charter
sigma run "fix the failing test in internal/foo" # one-shot
sigma chat # interactive TUI (--resume to continue) 
 run gates every mutating tool call for approval
 ( --yes auto-approves); read-only tools run without prompting. 
 The charter — your .sigma/ 
 A charter is the config bundle the agent loads from .sigma/ 
 (and ~/.sigma/ for user-global). It shapes behavior without
 touching code: 
 
 settings.json — model, permission mode, sandbox, plugins, compaction, event log 
 CLAUDE.md — instructions (root-down hierarchy; @path imports) 
 skills/ — on-demand skills (progressive disclosure) 
 agents/ — named sub-agent types (own prompt + tool subset) 
 styles/ — output styles (voice / behavior) 
 workflows/ — declarative multi-step / parallel orchestrations 
 commands/ — slash commands ( $ARGUMENTS expansion) 
 hooks.yaml — declarative lifecycle hooks (match + run / deny / log / notify) 
 
 Layers: sensors, guides, gates 
 
 Sensors — a typed event bus ( SessionStart , PreToolUse , PostLLMResponse , Stop , …) with a JSONL audit sink 
 Guides — the system prompt assembled from rules, skills, output styles, and agent-type prompts 
 Gates — permission modes ( default / acceptEdits / plan / bypass ), hook blocks, path rooting, git-worktree isolation, an OS sandbox (seatbelt / bwrap), and a code-health Stop gate that won't let a turn finish until tests/lint pass 
 
 Hooks can be declarative YAML , shell commands , or in-process
 Go callbacks — all on one bus. A Stop hook that exits non-zero
 makes the agent keep working until it's fixed. 
 Layers: a design methodology 
 Sigma leans into layers as its architecture — a dedicated middleware
 stack for an agent (Rack / Express / gRPC interceptors, but for a coding
 agent). The loop is a thin core; every cross-cutting concern is a typed layer
 wrapping one of three spines. A layer receives next and can
 observe , transform , short-circuit , or wrap — so a
 guard blocks, a cache returns early, redaction rewrites, a budget refuses. 
 
 Turn spine — wraps a whole turn: compaction → prompt-gate → loop 
 Model spine — wraps every model call: budget → retry → llm 
 Tool spine — wraps every tool call: … → ui → hooks → permission → exec 
 
 Plugins and charters contribute layers; ordering is the lever (canon
 guards before the sandbox, budget outermost). The stack is introspectable —
 agent behavior reads as a pipeline: 
 $ sigma layers
turn spine (outer → inner):
 compaction → prompt-gate → loop
model spine (outer → inner):
 budget → retry → llm
tool spine (outer → inner):
 dry-run → ui → hooks → permission → exec 
 Bec

bastion · software factory
how a job runs governance try it github

A software factory that runs on your own machine.

A request goes in, agents work it through a pipeline of stages, and a reviewed change comes out. Nothing merges itself: a person decides every merge. Each constraint and capability is a hook decision you can promote, demote, and test with an eval. It's early, though. The factory runs today, and the full pipeline is still being built.

Rust · Tauri 2 + Leptos · on iii 0.25.0 · macOS and Linux · one owner, no sign-in · status: phase A8 of 13

Try it Source Read the plan

Waiting for you2

divide: guard against zeroapprovelocal · demo-a · plan ready
close issue #1landlocal · ianparo/bastion · CI green

In progress2

count lines with wcbuildtwo · demo-b · turn 3
subtract: add a docstringreviewlocal · demo-a · 2 line comments

Finished2

multiplystoppedlocal · demo-a · VM gone
subtractlandedlocal · demo-a · 0e30e2f

An illustration of the Jobs page. Jobs that wait on you come first, and each one names its Bastion server.

How a job runs

A job is one request against one repository, like a ticket. It gets its own worktree, its own sandbox VM, and one pipeline run. The smallest pipeline has five stages:

plan approve build review land

Agent stages run turns in the sandbox. Person stages, marked ◆, are checkpoints where you decide. Each checkpoint has a dial: ask waits for you, hold waits 30 minutes and then goes on, and auto goes on at once. Merge never goes below hold.

Every stage leaves an artifact you can judge, such as a plan, a test result, or a diff. If you comment on one, the comment goes to the agent word for word as its next brief. A line comment on calc.py:5 comes back answered in the next diff. Fix loops stop after a set count, or sooner when the same refusal repeats.

The full pipeline adds scope, discovery, acceptance tests that must fail before the change and pass after it, a refactor pass, and a code review turn. That work is phase A8, and it isn't finished.

Governance you can measure

A rule that lives only in a prompt can't be measured. So in Bastion every rule is a hook decision, and its position on a ladder is data. You move a rule one rung at a time, and each move is recorded.

Constraint: what a turn must or must not do

toldThe rule is in the brief.
checkedA hook records each breach.
enforcedA hook refuses the call.

Capability: what a turn may call

deniedThe call is refused.
askThe call waits for you.
allowedThe call runs.
heldplan turn wants to write notes.mdcapability: ask
Allow onceRefuse

A held call. Allow once runs exactly that call. Refuse sends the refusal back to the agent.

Rules come from three layers. The charter is the repository's own, read from its .claude/settings.json and hooks. The harness binds each call in a turn. The factory binds review, land, pull requests, and merges. You edit the harness and factory rules on their pages while jobs run, and the gate reads them again before each turn.

Evals that show what a change does

An eval runs two harness configurations on the same requests and the same repository snapshot. Then it reports the difference, with the hook decisions behind it. Trial jobs stop at review, so nothing lands.

In one recorded run, three requests each asked for a wc count. Arm A had no-wc told, and arm B had it enforced. All six runs reached review.

MeasureA: toldB: enforced
Refused calls05
Review findings20
Turns3928
Tool calls3317
Cost$0.0344$0.0207
Grade77

Each refused call links to its audit entry. Apply B then promoted the rule, and the audit log recorded the move with the eval behind it. Three requests is a small sample, so read this as one result, not a benchmark.

An audit record that notices tampering

The audit log is a hash chain with one writer. Each entry carries an HMAC-SHA256 of its fields and of the entry before it. The key lives in the macOS Keychain, not in the database, so whoever can edit the database can't recompute the chain.

$ verifychain verified · 335 entries$ # change one byte of entry 20, then verify againchain broken at entry 20

The limits matter too. The chain detects a change, but it can't stop one, and it can't tell when entries were cut from the end. A remote append-only copy would close that gap, and it isn't built yet.

Bastion servers

The factory runs in bastion-server, one Rust binary. The app is a client that shows state and sends your decisions, so jobs keep moving with the window closed. The app starts a server on this machine, called local. You can add other Bastion servers, and each one holds its own repositories, each with its own setup, checks, and tests.

You pick the server when you start a job. The Jobs page lists the jobs of every server, and it says when one can't be reached.

Agent turns run in iii-sandbox VMs, and a credential never enters a VM. Pushes and pull requests happen on the host. The engine listens on loopback only.

What it is not

  • Not an editor. The only code you see is the diff a job proposes. "Open in editor" hands the worktree to your own editor.
  • Not an agent chat. You talk to a job through its artifacts and checkpoints, not a prompt box.
  • Not multi-user. One owner, no sign-in. The actor on each record is your git config user.name.
  • Not hosted. It runs on your machine, or on a box you own.
  • Not Windows. Sandbox VMs need Apple Silicon or Linux with /dev/kvm.

Try it

You need these first:

  • Rust from rust-toolchain.toml (rustup picks it up), and the wasm32-unknown-unknown target.
  • cargo install tauri-cli trunk
  • iii 0.25.0 on your PATH.
  • A model provider key, such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY, in the environment you start Bastion from.
  • gh, signed in, for pushes and pull requests. Landing locally works without it.
git clone https://github.com/tacoda/bastion
cd bastion
cargo tauri dev

Then go to Engine and press Start. Bastion runs Doctor and brings up the stack. If something is missing, Doctor names it and says how to fix it, and a failed required check stops the start.

Start one job on a small repository this week, and comment on its plan before you approve it. PLAN.md has the phases and says which layer owns what.

Bastion is by Ian Johnson · github.com/tacoda/bastion

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/tacoda/.claude/skills/voice-check

# Voice check

**`~/.claude/VOICE.md` is the standard and the only source of truth. Read it
first, every time. Do not review from memory of it, and do not restate its rules
here.** This file only covers how to run the check.

This is the authoritative stage of the VOICE.md section 15 chain, and the only
one that rewrites nothing. `humanizer` handles tone and `slopbeth` handles slop,
but both rewrite, so both can hand back what this skill already rejected. That
is why it runs first to set the constraints and again at the end as the gate.

It also catches what neither of them can: Ian's own formula, and drift between
pieces.

## Steps

1. Read `~/.claude/VOICE.md`.
2. Run the checker:
   ```bash
   python3 ~/.claude/skills/voice-check/voicecheck.py PATH \
     --corpus ~/tacoda/tacoda.github.io
   ```
   `PATH` takes a file or a directory. HTML is stripped to prose; code blocks,
   styles and scripts are excluded. `--corpus` enables recycled-phrase detection
   against the published body of work. Exits non-zero when there are findings.
3. Add `--show-flow 2` to print the paragraphs where sentences stop connecting.
   That is the fastest way to fix what reads as cold.
4. Run `humanizer` for tone, then `slopbeth` for slop, then this checker again
   as the gate. Both rewriters run under the findings from step 2 as hard
   constraints: neither may reintroduce a banned phrase, an em dash, or a tic
   already over budget, and neither may add a claim, number, or first-person
   experience the draft does not already contain. A finding that reappears at
   the gate gets fixed in the rewriter that put it back.
5. **Read the prose.** The script reports signals, not judgment. It cannot see a
   section that answers no reader question, an aphorism doing the work a
   mechanism should do, or a missing concession.
6. Report or fix, per what was asked, quoting the exact span for each finding.

## Reading the output

Findings marked `[advisory]` are the deliberate-structure cases in VOICE.md §5:
parallel rubric labels, non-goals lists, data triads. They usually mean leave it
alone. Everything else is a real finding.

Two metrics are easy to misread:

- `reader address` counts "you"/"your" **and** imperatives, so a page of
  instructions scores correctly without contorting into second person.
- `flow` is measured only inside paragraphs of three or more sentences. A
  reference page made of tables and captions is not scored on it.
- `over length` counts body prose only, so a page sitting near the 4,500-word cap
  is longer than that in wall-clock time once its code blocks and tables are
  read. VOICE.md §16 says what to cut and in what order.

## Rules

- **Preserve every fact.** Numbers, counts, dates, repo names, stated
  uncertainty, and non-goals survive any rewrite.
- **Never invent** first-person experience to hit the "I" floor. That floor is a
  request for a fact only Ian has. Ask him for it.
- **Do not trade one formula for another.** Replacing negation-definitions with
  clipped aphorisms is not a fix, and splitting a joined clause into two flat
  sentences to kill an em dash makes the prose worse, not better.
- **Over-editing strong prose is a failure.** Targets are ranges, not gates. A
  deliberate violation that serves the reader is fine; say why in the report.

content.text:
I created the `gh-pages` branch and committed the Bastion product page to it. I have not pushed it yet. The branch is local only, in a worktree at `/Users/tacoda/tacoda/bastion-gh-pages` (commit `ef37c4f`), so `main` is unchanged.

**The page:** one self-contained file, `index.html`, plus `.nojekyll`, the same layout as the open-refinery and ghola branches.
- **Style:** I used CONTROLROOM. Your five reference pages already use PLEXUS, DAYLIGHT, SEAFOAM, and two light and dark looks of their own, and no product page uses CONTROLROOM. It is also the job-board look, which matches the Bastion app.
- **Sections:** an illustrated Jobs page board, how a job runs, the constraint and capability ladders with a held call, the A6 eval numbers (refused 0 → 5, cost $0.0344 → $0.0207), the audit chain and its limits, Bastion servers, non-goals, and setup steps.
- **Sources:** every claim comes from `README.md` or `PLAN.md`. The job board, the held call, and the audit output are mock-ups, and each one has a caption that says so.

**Checks:**
- `/voice-check` passes except for one item: the median sentence is 12 words, against a target of 13 to 18. I left that alone because it suits a short product page. I fixed the flow and passive-voice findings.
- I did not run `/humanizer` or `/slopbeth`.
- I rendered the page at 1280px and 390px. Nothing scrolls sideways at phone width.

**Publishing:** pushing the branch makes the page public at tacoda.dev/bastion. To publish, run these:

```sh
git -C ~/tacoda/tacoda/bastion push -u origin gh-pages
gh api -X POST repos/tacoda/bastion/pages -f 'source[branch]=gh-pages' -f 'source[path]=/'
```
